The Book uses a similar formulation when it commands the Israelites to bow with those who bow down (2:43), and the repetition of the formula for a woman in a sanctuary shows how the Book conceives of devotion: an individual practice embedded in a community's practice. A person's worship is not measured by its originality, and the reference point for it is the community that has been worshipping the same way.

**The Congregation the Command Assumes**

The instruction to bow with those who bow carries a setting inside it. Mary is told to join a body of worshippers rather than to perform an act on her own, and the Book uses the same phrase when it commands the community to bow down with those who bow down (2:43). The sanctuary in which she had been placed was served by a company of men, and the command places her among them in the act of worship.

The Book describes the House that Abraham and Ishmael were told to purify as a place for those who circle it, meditate in it, and bow and prostrate themselves in prayer (2:125). The two postures named in this verse therefore belong to a form of worship older than the community that reads the passage, and the command given to Mary is phrased in its vocabulary. Nothing in the sentence restricts the instruction by gender or by age. What it asks for is participation in the worship of the house where she had been dedicated, and the sūrah gives the command as the direct answer to the announcement of her election.
verses.44:
> This is news of the unseen that We reveal to you ˹O Prophet˺. You were not with them when they cast lots to decide who would be Mary’s guardian, nor were you there when they argued ˹about it˺

**Ghayb: What "the Unseen" Covers**

The verse describes what it has just narrated as news of the unseen, and the Arabic word behind the phrase is *ghayb*, which covers everything absent from human perception: what is hidden in space, what is past, what is still to come, and what belongs to another order of being altogether.

The Book uses the term for revelation's content throughout. At Sinai, the Prophet is told that he was not present on the western side of the mountain when the commandments were entrusted to Moses, nor was he there in his time (28:44). The story of Joseph is introduced as one of the narratives of the unseen which God reveals to him, adding that neither he nor his people knew it beforehand (12:102; 11:49). The same construction frames the narrative of these verses about Mary. What the Prophet recites is knowledge he has no means of possessing, and the Book presents that fact as part of its claim.

**"You Were Not With Them" — an Argument From Absence**

The proof is stated as a fact about the Prophet’s biography, and its plainness is the argument. He was not among the priests of the sanctuary when they made their decision, and he was not present at their dispute. He was born centuries later, in a region where these events were not recorded and where the surviving traditions of the Jewish and Christian communities were not available to him in their original languages.

The argument that follows from this is not that a man could never have heard a story at second hand. It is that this particular narrative, in this detail, with its cast of characters, its procedure of casting lots, its setting, and its outcomes, did not exist in his environment. The Book's repeated use of the formula turns a narration into a testable claim: a reader may ask where the material came from, and the text itself invites him to.

**The Casting of Lots in a Sanctuary**

The verse refers to a procedure: the men concerned cast lots to decide which of them would take charge of the girl. The Book mentions a similar practice in the story of Jonah, who drew straws with the passengers of a ship and lost, and was thrown overboard (37:141).

The practice was well established in the region, and the accounts of it in other scriptural traditions show it used for a range of decisions — the allotment of duties among priests, the selection of animals for sacrifice, and the choice of a king. What concerns the verse's readers is the underlying conviction: a matter is referred to God by a procedure that removes human preference from the outcome. The guardian of a girl in the sanctuary was chosen that way, which means the community's most desirable responsibility was settled by something other than influence.

**Who Was Disputed, and on What Grounds**

Commentators recorded two views about the dispute. The majority held that the priests of the sanctuary wanted to be Mary's guardian and cast lots to determine who would have the privilege, and that God's will gave her to Zachariah. Al-Ṭabarī preserved a second view in which Zachariah's position was not contested at all, since he was related to Mary's mother, and the dispute concerned other aspects of her care or of who would serve her in the sanctuary.

The first view is supported by the narrative's emphasis on the lots and by the role that Zachariah's care plays in the surrounding verses. The second view rescues the story from an apparent awkwardness, since a prophet competing by lot for a child's custody invites questions. The majority position is the stronger reading of the text: the verse states plainly that they cast lots and that they disagreed, and it treats the disagreement as a fact of the story rather than as something to be explained away.
verses.45:
> ˹Remember˺ when the angels proclaimed, “O Mary! Allah gives you good news of a Word from Him, his name will be the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary; honoured in this world and the Hereafter, and he will be one of those nearest ˹to Allah˺

**"A Word From Him" — the Phrase and What It Carries**

The child is called a word from God, and the phrase has occupied commentators and theologians since the earliest generations. The Book uses the same language elsewhere when it addresses the People of the Book: the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, is described as the fulfilment of God's Word through Mary and a spirit from Him, in a verse that immediately forbids the extremes of doctrine (4:171).

Commentators explained the phrase in several ways. Some read it as a statement about the means by which God's command became manifest in the world, comparing it to the way a ruler's justice may be said to be present in his deputy; others linked it to the fact that Jesus came into being by the command "Be" without the ordinary cause, so that his association with the word is direct and unmediated. The sūrah itself does not press an explanation; it states the honour and, three verses later, states the means, and it leaves the reader with both.

**"Honoured in This World and the Hereafter"**

The child is promised honour in both worlds, and the promise covers the whole span of his story. In this world, the Book says, God delivered him from those who disbelieved and elevated his followers above the deniers until the Day of Judgment (3:55), and the record of his miracles is preserved in the scripture he brought.

In the Hereafter the honour is stated in the same Book that insists on his servanthood: he is a servant whom God favoured and made an example for the Children of Israel (43:59). The two descriptions belong on one page. The Book's presentation of Jesus is consistently double: extraordinary in his birth and station, a servant in his relation to God, and it never lets either half of that description displace the other.

**"One of Those Nearest to Allah"**

The last phrase names a company: those brought near. The Book calls the foremost believers the ones nearest to God (56:11), and the same category is used of the blessed in the Hereafter, whose record is witnessed by the nearest to God and whose drink flows from a spring reserved for them.

Being placed in that company is the highest honour the sūrah can name, and it is worth reading carefully because it is a ranking within creation rather than a statement about divinity. The company has members. A person does not join a company by being its origin; he joins it by being brought near to someone else, and the phrase itself says so. What the announcement promises the child is proximity to God, which is the promise made to the righteous generally, in the sharpest form available.

**Servant and Sign: How the Sūrah Holds Both Together**

The chapter will repeatedly insist on a description that the announcement's language might appear to soften. Jesus speaks in the cradle and identifies himself, in the words the sūrah records elsewhere, as a servant of God who has been given scripture and prophethood (19:30).

Holding the honour and the servanthood together is what makes the sūrah's Christology coherent. A being created by a command, born of a woman, sustained by God's provision, who speaks as an infant and returns to his Lord, is a sign; and a sign is only a sign if it points away from itself. The announcement in this verse is the sūrah's fullest statement of what he was given, and the next two verses supply the conditions of his birth and the record of his speech.
verses.46:
> And he will speak to people in ˹his˺ infancy and adulthood and will be one of the righteous.”

**A Child Who Speaks, and Speaks as His Own Witness**

The verse closes the angelic announcement with a promise about the child's speech: he will speak to people in infancy and in adulthood. The infancy clause is the one that carries the sign, and the Book attaches it to a specific situation which the sūrah of Maryam narrates, where the child in the cradle answers the accusations being made against his mother.

The scene in that sūrah gives the miracle its purpose. A woman returns to her people with an infant and is met with the worst accusation a community could make of her; the Book records her response as a gesture, and then has the child speak for himself: he identifies himself as a servant of God, given scripture and prophethood, made a blessing wherever he goes, and commanded to prayer and alms for as long as he lives (19:30–31). The first recorded utterance of Jesus in the Qur'an is an argument in his mother's defence.

**"In Infancy and Adulthood" — the Two Stages as One Promise**

The promise names two stages and so covers a life rather than an episode. Infant speech would be a wonder on its own; a lifetime of speech after it makes the wonder a pattern, and the sūrah of the Table describes exactly that, when God reminds Jesus of His favour in supporting him so that he spoke to people in his infancy and in his maturity (5:110).

The pairing also answers a reader's suspicion. A single early miracle could be dismissed as a wonder story with no consequence; the Book presents the cradle speech and the adult ministry as two halves of one reliable account.

**"And One of the Righteous" — the Company He Belongs To**

The verse ends by placing him among the righteous, the same phrase used of John in verse 39 and of the prophets listed elsewhere in the Book. In the sūrah of the Cattle, Zachariah, John, Jesus, and Elias are named together as men who were all of the righteous (6:85).

The phrase is unremarkable in itself and consequential in this sūrah, because it is the Book's ordinary description of prophets. The child announced by angels, honoured in two worlds and brought near to God, is described with the same words used of his cousin and of the prophets of Israel. Whatever else the sūrah's readers conclude about him, they are given the category he belongs to.

**The Tradition of Those Who Spoke in the Cradle**

The Prophet's own report limits the wonder to a very small number. Abū Hurayrah heard him say: *None spoke in cradle but three: Jesus, Juraij, and a child* — and the report goes on to tell the story of the second, a hermit wrongly accused by a woman and vindicated by the speech of her infant, and of the third, a baby who answered his mother's wishes with a prayer that he not be like a tyrant and, in another case, that he be like a woman falsely accused (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3436).

The report does not diminish Jesus' sign; it places it inside a small category of divine interventions on behalf of the slandered. The two accompanying stories are both about false accusation and vindication, and the third involves a child who asks to be like a woman who is lied about rather than a man of power. The Book's tradition treats the cradle speech as evidence given by God for the innocent, which is precisely the role it plays in the sūrah of Maryam.
verses.47:
> Mary wondered, “My Lord! How can I have a child when no man has ever touched me?” An angel replied, “So will it be. Allah creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, ‘Be!’ And it is

**The Mother's Question**

The announcement has been given, and Mary answers it with a question about how it can happen. The fuller account in the sūrah of Maryam records the objection in her own words, including her insistence that no man has touched her and that she is not unchaste (19:20).

The phrasing she uses is important for the way the Book treats her. She is not asking whether God can do it; she is asking how it is to be done, and she clears her own reputation in the same breath by ruling out the two possibilities that a listener would assume. The question belongs to the same family as Zachariah's, asked a few verses earlier by a man who had also been told something impossible, and it is answered in much the same terms.

**"Allah Creates What He Wills"**

The clause that follows the agreement is a statement about creation, not about reproduction. The Book does not say that God will use an unusual means; it locates the event in the category of things God creates because He wills them.

The parallel account in the sūrah of Maryam carries the same reply with an addition: the matter is already decreed (19:21). Elsewhere the Book states the principle without a birth attached to it, so that the reader meets it as a doctrine rather than as an exception. What is being taught is a view of creation in which the divine will is a sufficient cause, and the annunciation becomes one illustration of a rule that governs everything that exists.

**The Command "Be" and What It Means for a Creature**

The verse then supplies the mechanism, and the mechanism is a word. When God decrees a matter, He tells it to be, and it is. The Book uses the formula for creation generally: the Originator of the heavens and the earth says to a thing *Be*, and it is (2:117); the same words describe His action in the sūrah of the Bees, of the Bee's Lord who says to what He wills to exist, *Be*, and it is (16:40).

The sūrah of Maryam uses the formula in a passage that forbids the very conclusion the annunciation might invite: it is not for God to take a son, and when He decrees a matter He tells it to be (19:35). So the formula is a statement about power, and at the same time a statement about the distance between the one who commands and the thing that comes to be at the command. What is created does not become the creator by having been created directly.

**Placed Beside Adam**

The sūrah states the comparison outright a few verses later, where the example of Jesus before God is given as the example of Adam: created from dust, told to be, and he was (3:59). The pairing settles the question of what a miracle of origin proves.

Adam had no parents at all; Jesus had a mother and no father; the rest of humanity has both. If the absence of a father were a claim to divinity, the absence of both parents would be a stronger one, and the Book's handling of Adam makes clear that being created directly is a statement about God's power rather than about the creature's status. The same formula covers both cases, and both men are servants.
verses.48:
> And Allah will teach him writing and wisdom, the Torah and the Gospel

**A Curriculum Announced Before the Birth**

The verse continues the angelic announcement and promises that the child will be taught. The verb is in the future, and it is attached to a person who has not yet been born: writing, wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel are his before anything has happened to him.

The Book's habit of describing prophetic preparation as divine instruction is consistent across its narratives. The Prophet of this sūrah is reminded that God has revealed to him the Book and wisdom and taught him what he never knew (4:113), and the community is told that the messenger recites God's revelations, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and wisdom (2:151; 3:164). The wording used for Jesus is the same as the wording used for Muhammad, which places both men in one category of recipients rather than two categories of being.

**"Writing and Wisdom" — the First Pair and the Question Behind It**

The first pair in the list has been discussed at length because the word rendered "writing" can also mean a book, and the sūrah has already used the same word for the Scripture given to Moses. Some commentators resolved the difficulty by taking the term here in its sense of the ability to write, since the Scripture given to Moses was centuries old and could not be something Jesus was taught as a new text.

**"The Torah and the Gospel"**

The two named scriptures are the revelation given to Moses and the revelation given to Jesus, and the sūrah has already described the second of them: the Gospel was given to Jesus as guidance and light, confirming what was revealed in the Torah and serving as a guide and a lesson to the God-fearing (5:46).

Placing both books in the list of what he was taught is the sūrah's way of fixing his position in the chain of revelation. He is taught the book that came before him, and he is given the book that will be associated with his name. He stands inside the sequence, receiving and then delivering, which is what every prophet in the Book does.

**Teaching as God's Act**

The verse's grammar keeps the initiative on God's side throughout. It does not say that Jesus learned; it says that God will teach him. The distinction is not pedantic, since the Book uses the same construction for the Prophet of this sūrah and for figures such as Luqmān, who was given wisdom by God without any account of how he acquired it (31:12).

The pattern tells the reader how to think about prophetic knowledge. It is not the product of study, though study is not despised in this religion; it is a gift that arrives complete enough to be relied on.

**The Other Verses That Pair the Book With Wisdom**

The pairing named in this verse is one the Book uses when it describes what God gives to a messenger. The community is told that a messenger has been sent among them to recite the revelations, purify them, and teach them the Book and the wisdom (2:151), and the same gift is described as the favour shown to the believers with the addition that they had previously been clearly astray (3:164). The descendants of Abraham are said to have received the Book and the wisdom along with great authority (4:54), which shows how old the pairing is.

The Gospel narrative uses it for Jesus, where God recounts the favour of teaching him writing, wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel (5:110), and the sūrah of the Kneeling mentions the Scripture, the wisdom, and prophethood as what was given to the Children of Israel (45:16). The list in this verse therefore belongs to a pattern the reader meets repeatedly: wisdom is named alongside the text rather than derived from it, and the two are given together by the same act.
verses.49:
> and ˹make him˺ a messenger to the Children of Israel ˹to proclaim,˺ ‘I have come to you with a sign from your Lord: I will make for you a bird from clay, breathe into it, and it will become a ˹real˺ bird—by Allah’s Will. I will heal the blind and the leper and raise the dead to life—by Allah’s Will. And I will prophesize what you eat and store in your houses. Surely in this is a sign for you if you ˹truly˺ believe

**A Messenger With a Named Audience**

The announcement now appoints the child to a mission and specifies the people it concerns: he is made a messenger to the Children of Israel. The Book states the same limit when it reports him speaking to that nation and identifying himself as God's messenger sent to them (61:6), a verse that goes on to say he announced a messenger coming after him.

The restriction is worth comparing with the mission given to the Prophet of this sūrah, which the Book describes as addressed to all of humanity (34:28), and with the declaration that he is God's messenger to all people without exception (7:158). The Qur'an does not blur the difference between the two commissions; it states each in its own terms and leaves both standing, and the reader is meant to weigh what each messenger was sent to do.

**"By Allah's Will" — the Clause Attached to the Miracles**

The phrase occurs twice in this verse, once after the bird and once after healing and resurrection, and it is repeated in the reminder at 5:110 with the divine voice saying "by My Will" at each healing and each raising. The pattern is too consistent to be incidental.

The clause does the central work of the sūrah's teaching about Jesus. A sign performed by permission belongs to the one who permits it, and the Book's insistence on the clause at the very moments a reader might conclude otherwise is a deliberate safeguard. It also matches the way the Book describes the Prophet's own miracles elsewhere: works beyond human power occur at the command of God, and the servant who performs them remains a servant.

**Healing the Blind and the Leper**

Two healings are named, and the terms used matter. The first describes a person blind in a way that most commentators took to mean blind from birth, since the Book uses the standard word for blindness elsewhere and a specific form here. The second describes the leper, a sufferer of a disease that produced severe disfigurement and nerve damage, was widely regarded as contagious, and remained incurable by medicine until the modern era.

The Prophet's teaching addressed the fear such illnesses produced in his own society: he rejected the idea that disease transmits itself independently of God's will, and he instructed people in the same report to keep away from a leper as one would flee from a lion (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5707).

**Raising the Dead**

The third sign is the greatest in the sequence, and it is named in a single clause. The Book repeats it in the reminder of favours: how he brought the dead to life, by God's permission (5:110). The claim is accepted in the sūrah as a fact about his mission, and the same claim is made in the Gospel accounts, so that a reader of either tradition meets it as familiar ground.

What the sūrah does with it is the same thing it does with the bird from clay: it states the act and attaches the permission. The Book has confronted the argument that such deeds prove divinity by the blunt method of repeating the qualifier, and it has already applied that method to the greater act of creation itself, where the one who says to a thing "Be" is God and the thing that comes to be is a creature.

**"A Sign for You If You Truly Believe"**

The verse closes with a condition, and the condition is the sūrah's recurring theme. The signs are called a sign for you, if you believe; the benefit of evidence depends on the disposition of the person receiving it.

The Book states that principle repeatedly. Signs and warners are of no benefit to those who refuse to believe (10:101), and the Prophet is told that if their rejection is unbearable he should consider that God could have guided them all without any of it, since signs are not what opens a heart (6:35). The list of miracles in this verse is therefore offered to a specific audience, and the Book is honest about what it can and cannot do. Evidence settles a case for a mind that has not already decided, and the miracles of a prophet are addressed to people who are willing to look at them.
verses.50:
> And I will confirm the Torah revealed before me and legalize some of what had been forbidden to you. I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, so be mindful of Allah and obey me

**Confirming the Torah, Once More**

The speech continues and returns to the theme the sūrah opened with. The messenger confirms the Torah revealed before him, which is what the Book says of the Gospel itself: We gave him the Gospel containing guidance and light and confirming what was revealed in the Torah (5:46). The same relation is stated of the Qur'an at the start of this sūrah, which comes confirming what was before it.

The sentence therefore places Jesus in a line rather than at a break. He does not arrive with a new religion that displaces what his people had; he arrives attesting it and correcting what had gone wrong in its handling.

**"I Will Legalize Some of What Had Been Forbidden"**

The second clause announces a change in legal content, and it says *some*: a portion of what had been forbidden is to be made lawful. Commentators discussed what the forbidden items were, and two explanations were recorded. On one reading they were the restrictions imposed on the Jews as a consequence of their conduct, which the Book describes when it says it forbade them certain foods that had been lawful and names the specific categories of animals and fats (4:160; 6:146). On the other, they were burdens the community had taken upon itself over the generations rather than obligations from God.

The first reading fits the context more closely, since the sūrah is describing what a messenger was sent to do for a people whose laws had become heavy. It is also supported by the Book's account of Jesus describing his mission as coming with wisdom to clarify some of what the people differed about (43:63), which corresponds to a correction of practice rather than the introduction of a new law. The two readings converge on a single fact: what the messenger loosened concerned rules of conduct within Israel's own tradition, and the change was announced as a relief.

**"So Be Mindful of Allah and Obey Me"**

The command couples the two obligations the sūrah has already joined in its instruction to the community: fear God and obey the messenger. The phrase itself is a formula of the prophets, and the Book puts it in the mouth of messenger after messenger — Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Lot, and Shuʿayb each say, in the sūrah that reports their missions, the same words: so fear Allah, and obey me (26:108; 26:126, and the parallel verses throughout that sūrah).

The uniformity is the point. A preacher of a new doctrine with a personal claim to obedience would be a person to distrust; a messenger who says what every messenger has said, and who asks for obedience in the same breath as mindfulness of God, is speaking in the register of revelation. The Book's prophets answer a people's question about authority in advance by making their claim identical across centuries.

**What the Confirmation Means Here**

The sentence places Jesus in a chain that the sūrah has already described in its second and third verses. He confirms the Torah, and the same verb is used of the Book given to the Prophet when it is said to confirm what came before it (2:41, 91, 97; 3:3; 4:47; 35:31; 46:30). Elsewhere the Gospel is said to confirm the Torah as well (5:46), and the same language appears once more when Jesus is described as confirming what was sent before him (61:6). The wording is therefore not a claim about Jesus alone; it is the Book's standard way of describing the relation between its messengers, each one affirming what his predecessor brought rather than replacing it.

**Which Rules Were Relaxed**

The phrase about making lawful part of what had been forbidden was referred by al-Qurṭūbī and al-Ṭabarī to dietary rules rather than to the foundations of the law, since the prohibitions of murder, theft, and adultery were not the subject of any relaxation. The restrictions in question were either part of what the Torah itself laid down, including the rules the Book mentions in the sūrah of Women and the sūrah of the Cattle (4:160; 6:146), or they were practices the Israelites had imposed on themselves in later generations, which is how Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭūbī read the verse that mentions what Israel forbade itself before the Torah was sent down (3:93). On the second reading Jesus changed nothing in the original revelation, and the statement in the sūrah of the Ornaments that he came to make clear some of the matters on which they differed supports it (43:63). Al-Ṭabarī recorded the view that what Jesus brought was gentler than what Moses brought, an alleviation rather than a new law, and the verse's wording allows for that description of the change.

**The Formula the Prophets Share**

The command to be mindful of God and to obey the messenger appears on the lips of several prophets in the Book. Noah speaks it to his people, and so do Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Lot, and Shuʿayb, each addressing his own community with the same pair of clauses (26:108, 126, 144, 163, 179). The declaration that God is my Lord and your Lord is likewise shared: Jesus says it in three other places in the Book (5:72, 117; 19:36; 43:64), Hūd says it to his people (11:56), and Moses says it to Pharaoh (40:27; 44:20). The verses of this passage therefore give Jesus the same words the earlier messengers used, which is the point the sūrah has been making about the unity of the prophetic message.
verses.51:
> Surely Allah is my Lord and your Lord. So worship Him ˹alone˺. This is the Straight Path.’”

**The Sentence That Closes a Prophet's Speech**

The verse ends a speech that began four verses earlier, and it ends on a creed rather than on a wonder. The list of signs has been given — the bird of clay, the healing of the blind and the leper, the raising of the dead, the knowledge of what is hidden in houses — and the speech closes with a single declaration about God.

That arrangement is the sūrah's argument in miniature. A messenger who performs signs that no human being can perform, and who then says nothing about his own status, has answered the question his signs raise before anyone asks it. The sentence he chooses to end on is not "I am" but "He is", and the conclusion he draws from his own miracles is an instruction to worship God.

**"My Lord and Your Lord" — One Lordship, Two Relations**

The words name a shared relationship without flattening it. God is the speaker's Lord and the hearers' Lord, which means both parties stand in the same position of dependence, and the difference between them lies in the mission, not in the nature.

The Book puts this phrase in the mouth of the same prophet on several occasions, and each time it answers a different error. In the sūrah of Maryam, Jesus declares that God is his Lord and theirs and that this is the Straight Path (19:36). In the sūrah of Ornaments of Gold the words are again his, followed by the same call to worship God alone (43:64). In the sūrah of the Table, the declaration is quoted as the answer to the claim that God is the Messiah: the Messiah himself said, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord (5:72). The verse under discussion is the sūrah's own statement of the same formula, and its placement inside the list of miracles is deliberate.

**Other Prophets Said the Same Words**

The phrase is not unique to Jesus, and every reader of the sūrah has heard it before. Moses uses the same pair of possessives when he seeks refuge: I seek refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant person who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning (40:27), and again when he asks not to be stoned (44:20). Hūd uses the form in the sūrah of Hūd, and the formula recurs throughout the missions recorded in the Book.

The uniformity is the point of revelation's presentation of the prophets. What every messenger announces is that God is the Lord of both speaker and audience, which makes the messenger a servant of the same Lord as the people he addresses. A prophet who stood outside that relation would be a different kind of being, and the Book does not have such a category.

**Worship as the Only Conclusion**

The instruction that follows the declaration is *so worship Him alone*. The particle connects the two sentences logically: because He is the Lord of both, worship is owed to Him by both. The sign and the command are bound together.

This is where the sūrah's treatment of miracles differs from a reader's expectations. The signs are not presented as proof of the messenger's elevation; they are presented as reasons to worship the one who permitted them. Everything a prophet does in the Book points away from himself, and a wonder that pointed toward the wonder-worker would be a different sort of event entirely. The healings and the raising of the dead in the previous verse lead to an imperative about God, and the transition is so natural that the reader may pass over how unusual it is.
verses.52:
> When Jesus sensed disbelief from his people, he asked, “Who will stand up with me for Allah?” The disciples replied, “We will stand up for Allah. We believe in Allah, so bear witness that we have submitted.”

**A Prophet Reading His Own People**

The verse begins with a prophet detecting something: when Jesus sensed disbelief from among his people, he asked a question. The word *kufr* here describes not a private opinion but a settled hostility, and the commentaries understood it as the point at which the rejection had become active — the hostility that made it necessary for him to look for support elsewhere.

The situation is the same one the sūrah's readers know from their own prophet's life, and the parallel is intended. The Book's messengers do not fail because their message is defective; they are refused by people who have already decided, and each of them reaches a moment where the question shifts from "will you believe?" to "who will stand with me?" The verse is therefore both a scene from the past and a pattern the sūrah has established.

**The Word They Use About Themselves**

The clause rendered "we have submitted" uses the participle, and the disciples by this take the same word the sūrah used of everyone who has handed himself over to God. The Book uses it of Abraham and Jacob advising their children, and of the disciples again in another sūrah where their declaration is recorded with the word for belief and the request for witness (5:111). The word is not the property of any later community; it is what a person is when God's claim has been accepted.

The choice of the participle rather than a stronger statement of identity is also worth noticing. The disciples do not claim a rank or a station. They describe a state, and they ask that the state be witnessed. It is possible to hear in their sentence the tone of people who know that a commitment is only as good as what follows it, and who therefore put it on the record while it can still be tested.

**The Same Exchange in Another Sūrah**

The Book recounts the disciples' answer a second time as part of a longer passage. The believers are told to stand up for God as Jesus asked the disciples, quoting the question and the answer and adding the sequel: a group of the Children of Israel believed and another disbelieved, and God supported the believers against their enemies so that they prevailed (61:14).

The sequel tells the reader what the exchange was for. The disciples' commitment was not an end in itself; it entered a contest that the Book describes as having a verdict, and the verdict was on the side of those who stood up. Setting the shorter account beside the longer one gives this verse its context: a small group of men answered a question in a moment of danger, and the Book records their answer twice.

**What a Faithful Answer Costs**

The verse's ending is a request for witness, and the request implies a future that will require the answer to be repeated. Believing and standing up are not one-time announcements, and the disciples knew they were asking to be held to what they had said.

For the community reading the sūrah in Madinah, the scene offered a model that its own circumstances made urgent. A message that is not accepted by the powerful will need people willing to say publicly what they have decided privately, and the disciples are shown doing exactly that while their prophet is being refused. The next verse records what they asked for.
verses.53:
> ˹They prayed to Allah,˺ “Our Lord! We believe in Your revelations and follow the messenger, so count us among those who bear witness.”

**A Prayer Built From the Preceding Verse**

The disciples have affirmed their belief and their support to the messenger; they now say the same things to God. The verse is their supplication, and its three clauses repeat, in the language of worship, the three clauses they had spoken to a human being.

That movement from a public commitment to a private prayer is the Book's ordinary pattern. A person declares his position among people, and then presents it before God, where the declaration is either confirmed or exposed. The disciples do both in the space of two verses, and the sūrah supplies no gap between the pledge and the prayer in which the pledge could be forgotten.

**"We Believe in Your Revelations"**

The first clause is belief, and the object is specific: what God has sent down. The Book uses the plural to cover the whole body of revelation given to the prophets, and the disciples' declaration places the earlier scriptures and the message of Jesus in one object of faith.

The wording avoids a narrowness that a reader might expect. These are men who belong to the community of Israel and who accept a prophet raised among them; their confession is not "we believe in our prophet" but "we believe in Your revelations". The distinction matters in a sūrah that repeatedly criticises people who accepted part of what they were given. The disciples' statement covers the whole; there is no portion of revelation they set aside.

**"Count Us Among Those Who Bear Witness"**

The request is unusual in its modesty and its precision. The disciples do not ask for reward, protection, or victory; they ask to be registered in a category. The category is *the witnesses*, and the Book uses it as one of its most honourable designations, applied to the community of the Prophet as a whole: you have been made an upright community so that you may be witnesses over humanity, and the Messenger a witness over you (2:143).

Bearing witness in this vocabulary carries two senses at once, and the sūrah's usage requires both. A witness is a person who knows something and a person who says what he knows, and the Book's witnesses are those whose lives attest what they have understood. The disciples ask to be counted — the verb is that of a clerk entering a name in a register — which means they are asking for something no effort can produce on its own. A person can perform acts; he cannot inscribe himself among the witnesses of God.

**Who the Witnesses Are in the Wider Book**

The theme is one of the sūrah's deepest concerns. At the opening of the passage about the witness-bearing community, God is called the foremost witness that there is no god but Him, with the angels and the people of knowledge testifying after Him (3:18). Later in the sūrah, those who refuse the invitation are invited to bear witness to the submission of the believers (3:64). The disciples' prayer in this verse slots into that structure: God witnesses to Himself, the learned witness to what they know, and a community of ordinary believers is asked to carry the same testimony before humanity.

The hierarchy is worth keeping in view, because it explains why being counted among the witnesses is such a serious request. A witness whose testimony is false does not merely lie about a fact. He contradicts the testimony of God, the angels, and those who know, which is why the Book treats a deliberate misstatement about God as the gravest of offences.
verses.54:
> And the disbelievers made a plan ˹against Jesus˺, but Allah also planned—and Allah is the best of planners

**Makr: the Word Both Sides Share**

The Arabic verb behind both halves of the sentence is *makara*, and using one word for the plotting of the enemies and for the action of God is a rhetorical choice the Book repeats elsewhere. The conspirators against the Prophet of this sūrah are described in the same terms: they plotted to capture, kill, or expel him, and the verse ends with the same declaration that God is the best of planners (8:30).

The Book uses the word freely of God, and it does not soften it into a different verb to protect a doctrine of divine conduct. What it does instead is to repeat the comparison in a range of contexts — 13:42 where the earlier communities planned and God had the ultimate plan, 27:50 where a plan was made and a plan was made in return while the plotters were unaware. Using one word for both keeps the contest intelligible: the same kind of activity is going on, with an unbridgeable difference of power and knowledge behind it.

**What God's Plan Was in This Case**

The sūrah states the answer three verses later, in the form of a reminder addressed to Jesus; other passages fill in the moment itself. The Book says of the conspiracy to kill Jesus that he was neither killed nor crucified as the plotters assumed, that those who argue for the crucifixion are in doubt about it, and that God raised him up to Himself (4:157–158).

The commentators connected this verse to that event. The plot was the removal of a messenger by execution, and the counterplan was the removal of the messenger by God, in a way that left the plotters holding their weapons and no body. The Book does not describe the mechanism, and it is careful not to concede the plotters' version of events even as it reports their planning. What the reader is told is that a scheme was made and answered, and the answer preserved the messenger's mission rather than ending it.

**"Best of Planners" — a Comparison, Not a Contest**

The closing phrase is a superlative, and superlatives about God in this Book are usually statements about quality rather than predictions about outcomes. God is the best of planners in the sense that His arrangements cannot be defeated, cannot be anticipated, and cannot be improved upon.

The word also removes a misunderstanding the previous clauses might create. Saying that God "also planned" could suggest a deity who reacts to human schemes, arriving late with a countermeasure. The superlative says otherwise: the plans of creatures are the small, visible movements in a design they cannot see, and the Book's habit of speaking of God's planning in the same vocabulary as human plotting is a concession to human capacity for understanding, not a description of two equals at a board. What looks like a contest from below is an arrangement from above.

**The Three Other Passages About Plotting**

The Book states the same contrast in three further places, and each of them supplies a detail the sentence here leaves out. The sūrah of the Ant tells the same story of a people who made a plan while an unseen plan was being made for them, and it notes that they were unaware of it (27:50).

Al-Rāzī and others read the words about God's planning here as a reference to what the next verse states: the taking of Jesus and his raising to God. The three passages together show how the Book handles the subject. The opponents' plans are described in the terms they chose for themselves, and the answer comes from the same vocabulary turned against them, so that the comparison in the verse before the reader — the best of planners — is presented as a fact about outcomes rather than as a boast.
verses.55:
> ˹Remember˺ when Allah said, “O Jesus! I will take you and raise you up to Myself. I will deliver you from those who disbelieve, and elevate your followers above the disbelievers until the Day of Judgment. Then to Me you will ˹all˺ return, and I will settle all your disputes

**God Speaking to His Servant**

The verse opens with a reminder of a conversation: when God said, O Jesus. The speaker is God and the addressee is the messenger, and the words that follow are a set of promises spoken at the moment the plot of the previous verse was in motion.

Placing the promises in God's own voice matters for how the passage is read. Everything here is a commitment made by the one who made the plan, and the reader is being shown the content of the countermeasure at the exact point where the sūrah has just told him that a countermeasure was made. The promises are delivered to the man in danger, and the sūrah records them in full.

**Mutawaffī: the Word That Carries the Dispute**

The first promise uses a word from the root that governs taking and completing, and the sūrah's translation renders it as taking to Himself. The commentators spent considerable effort on it, and their disagreement is worth setting out plainly. A large group held that the word ordinarily refers to death, that God takes a person to Himself at the end of his life, and that in this verse, in view of what the Book says about the crucifixion, it means God's removal of Jesus from the world rather than his death at the hands of enemies. Others held that the word does retain its ordinary sense here and that the verse describes God causing him to die. A third reading took it in the sense of sleep, comparing the verse that says God calls back souls by night (6:60) and the verse that says He takes the souls of people at their death and those who do not die during their sleep (39:42).

Each reading has a Qur'anic usage behind it. What is not in dispute is that the word places the whole matter in God's hands: whatever the taking is, the taker is the one being addressed, and no enemy appears in the sentence.

**"And Raise You Up to Myself"**

The second promise names an elevation, and the Book states the same event when it answers the boasts of the plotters: they did not kill him, and God raised him up to Himself (4:158). The two verses describe one act from two angles, one as the removal of a servant from a hostile world and the other as an ascent.

The phrase "to Myself" is the part that has drawn the most attention from the commentators. The Book uses it nowhere else of a human being at the end of a mission, and whatever it means in detail, it states a destination rather than a location. The promise to a man whose enemies were arranging his execution is that he will be brought near to the one who sent him, and the nearness is the answer to everything the plot intended.

**Purification From the Disbelievers**

The third promise is that God will clear him of those who disbelieved. The commentators gave the verb two senses that complement each other: freeing him from their power, and absolving him of the charges they laid against him. Both are needed if the verse is to answer the situation described.

The followers of Jesus had accused him of blasphemy and sought his death; the sūrah's readers knew what the community had said about his mother and about his birth. A promise that he would be freed from their grasp and cleared of their claims is the answer to a slander as well as to a threat, and the Book's later defenses of Mary and of her son belong to the same act. What God promises in this clause is that the record will be straightened out, and the sūrah's narrative is part of how that happens.
verses.56:
> As for those who disbelieve, I will subject them to a severe punishment in this life and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers

**The Speech Continues**

The verse remains inside the speech that began in verse 55, and it turns from the messenger to the people who refused him. The promises given to the servant are followed by the consequences prepared for those who rejected him, and the sūrah keeps both halves of the announcement in the same voice and the same passage.

Reading them together prevents a mistake that a reader might make with either half alone. A promise of deliverance to the messenger could be mistaken for a reprieve for everyone who opposed him, and a warning about punishment could be mistaken for a description of God's ordinary disposition toward a community. The verse states the second half plainly, in the same tone, so that the two parties to the dispute hear the outcome that concerns them.

**Punishment in This Life and the Next**

The punishment is described as severe and as falling in two places: the life of the world and the Hereafter. The Book applies the two-world pattern to both reward and punishment in several passages, and the commentators noted that the pairing is deliberate and consistent.

What the punishment in this life consists of is left unspecified here, and other passages fill in the range: military defeat and displacement, the loss of the standing a community relied on, and the internal divisions that follow when a doctrine outlives the ability to defend it. The important element for the verse's argument is that the reckoning is not postponed entirely to another world. The Book describes a God whose judgments operate inside history, and the sūrah has already offered the fate of the people of Pharaoh as the proof that they do.

**"They Will Have No Helpers"**

The closing clause is the one that gives the sentence its weight. The sūrah used the phrase earlier for the deeds of a particular group being wasted, and it recurs across the Book in warnings about the Day of Judgment. A helper in the vocabulary of the Qur'an is not a friend in the ordinary sense; he is the person whose support changes what happens to you.

The world these verses describe was organised around exactly that relationship. A person's security depended on having parties who would defend him, ransom him, or plead for him, and a community's standing depended on the allies it could call on. The verse removes the whole apparatus: no clan, no patron, no protector, no intercessor, and no arrangement that could be made in advance. What remains is a case heard by a judge no one can influence, on a matter that the accused party has already decided.

**Who the Verse Addresses**

The sentence is introduced in the previous verse's frame as being about those who disbelieved, within the dispute over Jesus that occupies this part of the sūrah. The commentators understood it as covering the people who actively rejected him, and they read the severity as proportionate to the evidence they had refused.

The Book does not treat all disbelief as equivalent, and neither do the commentators. The severity in this verse is attached to a rejection made in the presence of a messenger, a message, and signs that the rejecters themselves had witnessed. That is the situation the Book consistently describes as the point at which a community's case is closed, and the tone of the sentence matches the situation rather than expressing a general disposition.

**Two Arenas of Recompense**

The sentence names this life and the Hereafter together as the places where the punishment of the rejecters is meted out, and the same pairing appears in several passages. One verse speaks of those who are disgraced in this world and have a severe punishment in the next (2:114); the sūrah of the Family of ʿImrān makes the same statement earlier in its own words (3:22); and the sūrah of the Bee speaks of the evil of this life and the punishment of the Hereafter as two parts of one outcome (16:30). The two arenas are described for the believers in corresponding terms, since the Book promises good in this world and a better reward in the next to those who act well (16:122; 39:10). The verse therefore does not present the worldly suffering of a people as proof of its standing, nor worldly ease as a sign of favour.
verses.57:
> And as for those who believe and do good, they will be rewarded in full. And Allah does not like the wrongdoers.”

**The Other Half of the Sentence**

The previous verse stated the end of those who disbelieved; this one states the end of those who believed and did good. The two form one sentence in the original sequence, and the sūrah gives the reward the second position, so that the passage closes on the group it hopes its readers will join.

The construction is familiar from the Book's treatment of the Day of Judgment, where the two outcomes are normally stated together. What deserves attention here is the order and the proportion. The warning occupies a full sentence about punishment in two worlds and the absence of helpers; the promise occupies a shorter sentence about full reward, and a clause about God's disposition that does not contain the word reward at all.

**"Rewarded in Full"**

The verb behind the phrase describes the payment of a wage in full, without deduction, and the Book applies it to the settlement of every soul's deeds on the Day of Judgment in several passages. Used here of believers, it carries an implication the reader should not miss: the reward is presented as a payment owed, an obligation the giver has taken upon himself.

The Book's language about reward goes further in other places, offering multiplication beyond measure, gifts without reckoning, and increases out of God's grace. Setting those verses beside this one shows how the Book holds two things together: what is owed is paid in full, and what is given exceeds what was owed. A servant who has done little and receives much is not being treated unfairly; he is dealing with a giver whose account of the transaction is generous rather than exact.

**A Reminder About Who Is Being Described**

The verse is often read as a general statement about the destiny of two classes of people, and it functions that way. In its immediate setting, though, it concerns the parties to a specific dispute: the community that rejected a prophet and the community that accepted him and acted on the acceptance. The word translated "wrongdoers" is not a synonym for "disbelievers" in every Qur'anic passage, and here it describes the members of the rejecting party whose conduct earned the description.

The distinction matters because the sūrah will go on, in the following verses, to make a very particular argument about what belief in Jesus requires. The reward described here is not offered to a category of people defined by their ancestry or their community affiliation. It is promised to those whose faith found expression in acts that the Book considers good, which is a condition that any reader of the verse can measure himself against.
verses.58:
> We recite ˹all˺ this to you ˹O Prophet˺ as one of the signs and ˹as˺ a wise reminder

**"We Recite It to You"**

The verb describes a recitation taking place in the present, and the Book uses it for the act by which revelation is delivered to the Prophet. The same verb appears at the openings of sūrahs where the revelation is being called to the reader's attention, and it places the Prophet in the position of a hearer rather than an author.

The construction has a doctrinal edge in a sūrah that has just been arguing with communities who possessed scriptures. A messenger is being told that the stories of the previous messengers are being recited to him by God, which means his knowledge of them is direct rather than inherited. Every narrative in the Book is presented as coming from the same source as the ones that came before, and the word "recite" keeps that claim alive at the level of the sentence.

**The Two Descriptions: Signs and a Wise Reminder**

The verse calls what it has recited two things. First, the material is a sign, and the Book uses that word for both the verses of revelation and the events of the natural world; both are described as things put in front of a person to be read. Second, the whole of it is a reminder that is wise, and the commentators noted that this phrase is used elsewhere as a name for the Qur'an, with some taking it to refer to the Preserved Tablet from which revelation comes down.

The two descriptions answer two purposes. A sign instructs by pointing at something beyond itself, and the disputes about Jesus, the plots, and the promises all point at the God who governs such matters. A reminder instructs by bringing back what is known, and the sūrah has been reminding its readers of truths their own traditions contained. Both descriptions apply to the passage the reader has just finished, and while the first of them requires him to think, the second requires him to remember.

**Where the Sūrah Goes From Here**

This verse marks the end of the section that began with the announcement to Mary, and the two verses that follow it address the Prophet directly about what belief in Jesus requires. The sūrah moves from the past to the present, and from the story to the disputants who had raised the story as an argument.

That transition is worth noticing because it explains the use of "we recite" here rather than at the start of the narrative. The sūrah has no interest in telling the story of Jesus for its own sake; the account is being delivered specifically to the man who will have to answer the community that disagrees with him about Jesus, and to the community that will have to hold its position. The verse states the source of the material at the moment the material is about to be put to work.
verses.59:
> Indeed, the example of Jesus in the sight of Allah is like that of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, “Be!” And he was

**Why Adam Is the Decisive Case**

The choice of Adam rather than another figure is deliberate, and it is worth seeing what the comparison does that a comparison with, say, Isaac would not have done. Isaac had a father and a mother, one of whom was beyond the age of childbearing; his case would have been an example of God overcoming a natural obstacle. Adam's case is categorically different: he had no parents at all, and his existence began with dust and a command.

If being created without a human father is evidence of divinity, then Adam has the better claim to it, since he was created without a human ancestry entirely. Since nobody makes that claim for Adam, the inference from the virgin birth collapses. The Book's argument is thus not that the miracle did not happen; it is that miracles of origin are statements about the one who makes them.

**Dust and the Command**

The verse describes the creation of Adam in two stages: God created him from dust, then said to him, Be, and he was. The Book states the same creation in its opening sūrah, where the creation of the first man is followed by the account of his knowledge and the prostration of the angels, and the phrase is used consistently to describe a bringing-into-being that has no process.

The two elements of the sentence belong together. Dust is the material, and it has no life in itself; the command is the act, and it has nothing in it that requires the cooperation of what it addresses. The Book's picture of creation is that God's speech is sufficient for anything to exist, and this verse applies the picture to the very beginning of the human race so that the reader can measure the nativity of Jesus against it.

**The Formula "Be" Throughout the Book**

The command appears in the Book wherever creation is described, and its repetitions form one of the Qur'an's most consistent themes. The Originator of the heavens and the earth, when He decrees a matter, tells it to be and it is (2:117). God's affair, when He wills something, is to say to it Be and it is (36:82). He who created the heavens and the earth in truth will say on the Day of Judgment Be and it will be (6:73), and the same words describe the giver of life and death when He decrees a matter (40:68). In the sūrah of the Bee, the formula states that God's command, when He wills a thing, is a single word (16:40).

Placing this verse in that series shows that the creation of Jesus is not an isolated exception but an instance of the way God has always acted. The Book's doctrine of creation is that existence follows a command, and the fact that a particular existence had an unusual origin is a difference in the circumstances, not in the kind of act.

**The Argument Answered Before It Was Made**

The sūrah's account of the delegations from Najrān and their arguments about Jesus is given in the opening of the chapter, and this verse is the Book's central rebuttal of the position they took. The rebuttal is brief, and it is complete.

What the reader is left with is a pattern of reasoning that can be used wherever the question arises. The Book acknowledges the wonders of a prophet's life without adjusting its account of God, and it defends both by placing the wonder inside the doctrine of creation. The verses that follow draw the conclusion and address the disputants directly.
verses.60:
> This is the truth from your Lord, so do not be one of those who doubt

**An Address Directed at the Prophet**

The verse changes addressee again and speaks to the Prophet of the sūrah about the account he has just received. What has been recited about Jesus, his birth, his mission, and the comparison with Adam is described as truth from his Lord, and the sentence closes with a prohibition against doubt.

The combination of a statement and a warning in one sentence is characteristic of the Book's manner with its own messenger. The Prophet is not excused from the demand the revelation makes on everyone who hears it, and the Book's treatment of him throughout contains warnings as well as commendations. A messenger who is told not to doubt is a messenger who is being held to the same standard he is delivering.

**"Truth From Your Lord"**

The phrase identifies both the content and its source. What has been recited is true, and it comes from the Lord of the person addressed, which places the Prophet in the same relation to God as the readers of the Book.

The construction recurs when the Book wants to end a discussion with a verdict rather than an argument. In the sūrah of the Cow, after the change of the direction of prayer and the disputes it produced, the verse states that what has come to them is the truth from their Lord and that they should not be among those who doubt. The sūrah here states the same formula at the close of the dispute about Jesus, and the effect is to remove the question from the plane of debate and return it to the plane of revelation.
verses.61:
> Now, whoever disputes with you ˹O Prophet˺ concerning Jesus after full knowledge has come to you, say, “Come! Let us gather our children and your children, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves—then let us sincerely invoke Allah’s curse upon the liars.”

**Who Was Brought to the Meeting**

The accounts differ in their details but agree on the essentials. The Prophet came out the next day for the appointment accompanied by his daughter Fāṭīmah and her two sons Ḥasan and Ḥusayn, and several accounts also include ʿAlī, her husband and the Prophet's cousin. Since the verse had named children, women, and selves, the party corresponds to the summons in each category.

The picture recorded in the tradition has become one of the most frequently cited scenes in later Islamic literature, and it is used to establish the standing of the household that was brought. The commentaries note that the Prophet brought no one else from among a large community, which the tradition reads as evidence of his confidence in the outcome. What the historical record shows without any interpretive layer is a small family group standing at an appointment that the other side did not keep.

**The Refusal and the Agreement**

The refusal of the challenge was followed by a settlement. According to the accounts, the Najrān delegation remained Christian, entered a treaty with the Muslim community, and undertook an annual payment, and the Prophet sent a trusted companion back with them at their request to serve among them as an arbiter.

The outcome is worth reading carefully, because it shows what the verses about challenge and curse were not. They were not an instrument of forced conversion. A community that declined the challenge and retained its religion kept its religion, and the terms that followed were political and financial rather than theological. The Book's argument about Jesus did not become an occasion for compulsion, which is consistent with the sūrah's own limitation of the Prophet's duty to delivering the message in the verses that came before this one.
verses.62:
> Certainly, this is the true narrative, and there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Allah. And indeed, Allah ˹alone˺ is the Almighty, All-Wise

**Where the Argument Leaves the Reader**

The verse ends the dispute about Jesus with a declaration rather than a rebuttal, and it does not address the disputants again. What follows turns to the community of the Book and to Abraham, and it begins a new phase of the sūrah's engagement with the claims of the scriptured peoples.

The two names with which the verse closes also tell the reader how to weigh the whole narrative he has just read. Almightiness explains why a birth without a father is possible; wisdom explains why such a birth was arranged for this prophet and not another. Both names are stated at the point where the account is declared true, as though the sūrah wanted the last thing said about the story to be a description of the one who decided it would happen. The accounts of the missionaries and merchants who carried these verses beyond Arabia belong to the history of the community; what the verse itself does is to hand the reader a fact about God and leave him to it.

Readers of the intervening centuries have found in these verses the summary of the Book's position on the nature of Christ, and the summary is complete on its own terms. The narrative is true, the deity is one, and the power and wisdom that arranged the birth belong to the one who arranged it. What the sūrah does next is to test the claims of the communities that disputed on the basis of an ancestor they shared with the Muslim community.

**The Formula Used Here**

The sentence has no god except God is not the wording of the community's standard testimony of faith. The usual formula begins with the negation of every deity and then affirms the one God; the version in this verse begins with the particle of restriction, and al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī described the construction as a stronger form of the negation. The difference is one of emphasis rather than of content, and the commentators noted it because the community's daily testimony uses the other wording. The choice of the stronger form here suits the sentence's position at the end of a dispute about claims made about God and His messengers, and it leaves the reader with the affirmation on which the whole passage rests.
verses.63:
> If they turn away, then surely Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the corruptors

**The Refusal Named Once More**

The verse follows the declaration of God's oneness with a conditional sentence: if they turn away, then God knows the corruptors. Three times in this sūrah the same refusal has been named, and each time the Book has responded differently — once by stating the duty of the messenger, once by naming the consequence in the language of divine disfavour, and here by referring the whole matter to knowledge.

The repetition traces the course of an argument that has been made and declined. The sūrah is not describing a fresh conversation; it is describing the position of people who have heard the recitation, the account of Jesus, and the creed, and have maintained their course. What the verse adds to the previous statements is a description of the refusal that is also a verdict, delivered as a fact about God rather than as a judgement passed by the messenger.

**A Conclusion That Opens the Next Section**

The verse closes the narrative block of the sūrah and opens the block that deals with Abraham. The subject is the same in both cases: which community has the better claim to the inheritance of a prophet.

The transition is smooth because the question has been prepared. The sūrah has just declared the truth of its account of Jesus and the oneness of God; it now turns to the ancestor whom the disputing parties shared with the Muslim community, and to the claim that he belonged to one of them. The refusers have just been described as people who spoil what they hold, and the next verses will show what they do with Abraham.
verses.64:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O People of the Book! Let us come to common terms: that we will worship none but Allah, associate none with Him, nor take one another as lords instead of Allah.” But if they turn away, then say, “Bear witness that we have submitted ˹to Allah alone˺.”

**An Invitation Addressed to the Scriptured Communities**

The sūrah turns from the dispute about Jesus to a direct address to the People of the Book, and the address begins with an invitation rather than a charge. The Prophet is told what to say, and what he says is *let us come*.

The form of the sentence is worth noticing before its content. An invitation belongs to a relationship of equals setting out to reach an agreed position; a proclamation would not have used the first-person plural. The invitation also treats the other party as capable of accepting it, since a call to agree on common terms would be pointless if the terms were not open to examination. The Book stages the encounter between the Muslim community and the communities that held earlier scriptures as a meeting in which the other party is asked to join the speaker on a shared footing. Nothing in the verse abandons the claim the sūrah has been making about the truth of its own account. What it does is to place the terms of agreement where both parties can recognise them.

**The Word Sawāʾ and What "Common Terms" Means**

The phrase rendered "common terms" translates a single Arabic word whose root sense is levelness, evenness, and fairness — the same root that gives the expression "the middle of the road" for the correct way of proceeding. The commentators found two readings, and they overlap more than they appear to.

Some took it to mean that the word being offered is a just and fair one, in the sense that both parties are treated equitably in it. Others took the term to describe what the two sides already share. Al-Rāzī's gloss captures the first reading well: come to a word in which there is fair treatment from each of us to the other. The translation's choice of "common terms" follows the second reading, and it fits the three items that follow, since each is a proposition that the earlier scriptures themselves assert.

**The Three Propositions**

The invitation names three commitments: worship of none but God, the association of nothing with Him, and the refusal to take one another as lords instead of God. The three form a single position stated from different angles.

The first two concern God directly, and they are the ground of everything the sūrah has said about Jesus: a messenger whose birth was a wonder is not a partner in divinity. The third concerns human authorities. The commentators offered two readings of it — that it forbids the prostration paid to religious leaders, and that it forbids obedience to them carried to the point of setting aside what is true. The Book states the same charge elsewhere in harsher language, describing people who took their rabbis and monks as lords apart from God, along with the Messiah, though they were commanded to worship one God (9:31). The clause in this verse is that criticism in the form of an invitation to its remedy.

**The Plural That Puts Both Sides Inside the Sentence**

The invitation is phrased in the first person plural: *let us come*, not *come*. The construction is unusual in the Book's addresses to those outside the community, and it does a specific piece of work. It places the speaker and the addressee inside the same sentence, so that the position being proposed is one that both parties are asked to take up together rather than one that the Prophet is imposing.

The closing clause completes the movement. When the other party refuses, the community is told to state its own position rather than to press the case further, and the word it is told to use is the one the sūrah has attached to the religion itself (3:19). The same word is spoken by Abraham and Jacob to their children in the sūrah of the Cow, where the father's advice ends with the instruction not to die except in submission (2:132). The verse therefore ends where the community's own confession lives, and it leaves the invitation standing as an offer whose terms were public.
verses.65:
> O People of the Book! Why do you argue about Abraham, while the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until long after him? Do you not understand

The verse addresses the People of the Book again, and it addresses them with a question about their own claim: why do you argue about Abraham? The dispute in view is a competition over which community may claim him, and the Book's response is to point at the calendar.

The argument is as simple as it is decisive.

**Ḥanīf: the Word for What Abraham Was**

The sūrah's account of what Abraham actually was comes in the next two verses, and the term at its centre is *ḥanīf*, a word the Book applies to a person who turns away from false worship toward the one God. In the vocabulary of the Qur'an it describes an inclination rather than a membership, and its consistent companion is the phrase "and he was not a polytheist".

The pairing appears throughout the Book's references to Abraham: the sūrah of the Cow gives the believers the creed of Abraham the upright, who was not of the idolaters (2:135); the sūrah of the Bees describes him as a model of excellence, devoted, upright, and not a polytheist (16:120); the sūrah of the Cattle gives the same formula in the Prophet's own declaration (6:161). The Book treats the term as a description of Abraham's actual religion before any community organised around a book, which is why it serves as the answer to a competition between those communities.

**A Shared Ancestor and a Shared Difficulty**

The argument in this verse cuts against both claimants at once, and the sūrah means it to. The Jews of Madinah and the Christians of the region each had a narrative of belonging that ran through Abraham, and each found in him a warrant for its own standing.

The Book's response refuses both moves by the same stroke: it denies that the ancestor can be claimed by a community whose distinguishing revelation came after him, and it does so without discarding him. Abraham remains central to the sūrah's argument — he is named among the chosen families at its beginning and will be discussed at length in the verses that follow. What the Book rejects is the use of his name as a deed of ownership, and it replaces that use with a description of what he believed. The question "whose was he?" is set aside and replaced by the question "what was he?", which the next verse takes up directly.

**What They Had Knowledge Of**

The first half of the question concerns matters that lay within the disputants' competence, and the commentators identified them in several ways. Al-Qurṭūbī and al-Zamakhsharī understood the reference to be their own scripture and the points on which they differed over it; al-Rāzī recorded the reading that it concerns what their laws permitted and forbade; and a further suggestion is that the dispute was about whether the new revelation agreed with or differed from the earlier books. All of the readings describe an argument conducted about material the parties possessed, which is why the verse can say that they had knowledge of it.

**The Claim About Abraham**

The second half of the question turns to Abraham, and the commentators are agreed that the disputants had no direct knowledge of him. Al-Qurṭūbī, al-Rāzī, and al-Ṭabarī all make the same point: he lived long before the books they possessed, and neither community could produce a record of his practice that settled the question. The verse's argument is therefore about the difference between two kinds of dispute, and the difference is one of evidence. A disagreement about texts a community holds can be conducted by examining those texts, while a disagreement about a man who preceded the texts requires something else, and the passage that follows supplies it by stating what Abraham actually was. The sentence leaves the reader with a rule that applies beyond the immediate dispute: the soundness of an argument depends on what the arguer can know.
verses.66:
> Here you are! You disputed about what you have ˹little˺ knowledge of, but why do you now argue about what you have no knowledge of? Allah knows and you do not know

**A Rebuke in Two Stages**

The verse takes the form of an observation about the disputants' own record: you argued about things you had some knowledge of, and now you argue about something you have no knowledge of at all. The sentence sets two disagreements beside each other and marks the difference in what the parties could bring to them.

The comparison is severe and it is made gently, in the manner of a person pointing out an inconsistency rather than delivering a verdict. The first dispute concerned matters within the community's competence — the interpretation of its own laws, the content of its own tradition, the points on which its own scholars differed. The second concerns Abraham, who lived long before the books they possessed and about whom their traditions carried no direct information. The verse's charge is that the habit of arguing has outlived the basis for it.

**What the Two Disputes Were**

Commentators offered several accounts of the disagreements in view. The matters the disputants had knowledge of were variously identified as their own scripture and the points at which they differed over it, the disputation over what their laws permitted and forbade, and the question of whether the new revelation agreed with or differed from the earlier books. The matter they had no knowledge of was their competing claims about Abraham, about which, as the sūrah has just pointed out, no direct report was available to them.

The distinction is one that any community with a tradition can understand. There is a difference between arguing from evidence within a field one has studied and arguing about a figure from a remote past on the basis of inherited pride. The verse does not dispute the community's competence in the first category. It points out that the second category has been treated as though it were the first.

**Disputing After Knowledge in the Sūrah's Other Sentences**

The distinction this verse draws is one the sūrah has been making since its opening pages. It states that the People of the Book did not dispute among themselves out of mutual envy until knowledge had come to them (3:19), and it warns the believers against becoming like those who divided and differed after the clear proofs had reached them (3:105). The Book returns to the same diagnosis in the account of the first community, which is said to have disputed the scriptures only after the proofs arrived, and to have done so out of jealousy (2:213).

In each of those sentences the arrival of knowledge is what turns a disagreement into a charge. The verse before the reader applies the distinction at a smaller scale, separating two arguments that the same people were conducting: one about material they possessed, and one about a man who lived before their books.
